notes.meaning: God gives Ezekiel a prophetic message in the final month of the twelfth year of exile. Jerusalem had already fallen to Babylon, and now God directs Ezekiel to speak about the coming ruin of Egypt. The timing showed both the exiles and the nations that God was completely in control of history.

Pharaoh viewed himself as a roaring young lion ruling the nations, but God describes him as a disruptive water monster like a crocodile. He thrashed through the Nile, stirring up thick mud and troubling the surrounding lands. God shows that proud rulers who bring chaos to the world are only wild beasts in His sight.

The Lord announces that He will capture this monster using a large net made up of many gathered nations. Babylon and its allied armies serve as God's tools to haul Egypt out of its safe waters. No human power is strong enough to escape God when He decides to act.

God drags the great sea beast onto dry land and leaves its carcass in the open fields for birds and wild animals to gorge on. Its flesh covers the mountains and piles high in the valleys, while so much blood pours out that it drenches the land up to the hills. This gruesome picture shows the total destruction of Pharaoh's armies and echoes the bloody plagues of old Egypt.

When God snuffs out the Egyptian ruler like a lamp, darkness spreads across the entire sky. The sun, moon, and stars are clouded over, blotting out their light above Egypt. This dark gloom represents the sudden collapse of royal power and points to God's terrifying day of judgment.

News of Egypt's sudden ruin will reach far-off countries and strike deep dread into many peoples. Nearby kings will shiver in horror as they see God swinging His sword of justice against so mighty an empire. Watching another proud nation fall reminds every ruler that their own lives hang by a thread.

God plainly identifies the instrument of His judgment: the king of Babylon and his ruthless warriors. Their sharp swords will cut down Egypt's massive crowds and strip away all the nation's treasured pride. Even the greatest worldly glory cannot protect a kingdom when God's appointed hour arrives.

God will destroy all the cattle that grazed beside the Nile, leaving no person or beast behind to churn up the river. With no one left to disturb them, the waters will settle and run clear, flowing slowly and quietly like oil. The stillness shows how thoroughly Egypt's bustling, troublesome power will be silenced.

Egypt will be turned into an empty wasteland, stripped of all its wealth, crops, and inhabitants. When the Lord smites the land, the survivors and neighbors will finally recognize His supreme power. Hard judgments often serve to teach a proud world that the Lord alone is God.

Ezekiel concludes the first prophecy by stating that the women of foreign nations will chant this funeral dirge over Egypt and her lost multitudes. Mourning the dead was usually done by women in the ancient world, and their sad song confirms that Egypt's fall is certain. Worldly greatness ends in weeping and regret.

Two weeks after the first message, God speaks to Ezekiel again on the fifteenth day of the twelfth month. This begins a second poem that pictures Pharaoh's descent into the realm of the dead. God repeats and expands His message so that His people will have no doubt about what is coming.

God commands the prophet to weep for Egypt's multitudes and to symbolically send them down into the pit of the earth alongside other fallen nations. By speaking God's word, Ezekiel declares the sentence that consigns this proud kingdom to the grave. Even the grandest empires must eventually descend to the dust.

The Lord challenges Egypt by asking if she thinks she is lovelier or better than any other kingdom that has already perished. Her royal splendor will not spare her from being placed among the uncircumcised, which meant dying a disgraceful, heathen death outside God's covenant. Death treats the proud just like everyone else.

Egypt is handed over to the sword of war and dragged away to the grave like an executed criminal. From Sheol, the dark place of the dead, other fallen warrior-kings call out to greet Egypt and her allies with bitter mockery. Those who once acted like gods on earth find themselves helpless and forgotten among the slain.

The mighty empire of Assyria is already lying in the deepest part of the pit, surrounded by the graves of all her slaughtered soldiers. That empire once terrorized the known world with ruthless violence, but its rulers were cut down in their prime. Those who live by causing fear eventually face the terror of death themselves.

The ancient warriors of Elam, known for their bows, are also buried in the pit with their fallen crowds. They once made the living earth tremble, but now they lie in shameful disgrace among those killed in battle. Their earthly fame has vanished, leaving only dishonor in the grave.

The northern peoples of Meshech and Tubal lie in the grave with all their multitudes. They were fierce, warlike nations who spread deep terror during their lives. Yet their savage strength could not save them from being cut down by the sword and buried in defeat.

These northern warriors do not receive the honored burial given to famous heroes of old, whose swords were tucked under their heads in state. Instead, they died in disgrace, and the weight of their sins rests heavily upon their fallen bones. A violent life brings no true honor at the end.

God turns directly to Pharaoh and warns him that he will be broken in the exact same way. Egypt's king will not escape the common fate of wicked tyrants, but will lie buried among the uncircumcised victims of war. God will bring down any ruler who refuses to humble himself.

Edom and all its fierce kings and princes are also gathered in the pit among the slain. Even though the Edomites descended from Abraham and were circumcised, their physical heritage could not shield them from sharing the fate of the ungodly. Trusting in past heritage or military might offers no shelter from God's righteous judgment.

The northern leaders and the Sidonian sea merchants are buried there as well, stripped of their former pride. Despite the fear their naval strength once inspired, they now bear the humiliation of the defeated in the grave. Human glory quickly fades when God calls nations to account.

When Pharaoh arrives in the realm of the dead and looks around, he will feel a grim, hollow comfort seeing that other powerful rulers have fallen too. Knowing he is not the first mighty king to be destroyed offers a tiny soothing of his wounded pride. Yet finding fellow sufferers in ruin is a poor, empty comfort.

The Lord states that He is the one who ultimately puts terror into the hearts of the living by judging ruthless tyrants. Pharaoh and all his vast army will be laid in the dust among the disgraced dead who were slain by the sword. God has the final word over every earthly power, and His justice will always stand.
